What this risk score actually guards against

Two confirmed DeFi thefts in 2026, both squarely in the risk class this oracle measures: a single compromised admin key, and an insufficient verification threshold on a cross-chain bridge.

$285M
Drift Protocol - 1 April 2026

An admin key compromised after months of social engineering (attributed to Lazarus/RPC-TraderTraitor) allowed the price oracles to be manipulated and the vaults drained within minutes.

adminKeyScore - exactly this axis
$292M
KelpDAO - 18 April 2026

A LayerZero bridge configured with a 1-of-1 verifier (DVN): a single node validated cross-chain messages before funds were released. Once compromised, it authorized the minting of 116,500 unbacked rsETH (~18% of the supply).

multisigScore / verification threshold - exactly this axis

What would a Safe multisig score?

Enter a Safe's threshold and owner count. This applies the convention the scorers use for a target whose whole authority chain ends in one plain Safe with no timelock, then places the result among the published scores and the documented incidents (four incidents, five Safes: Humanity Protocol lost funds from two Safes in one event). The two thefts in the panel above, Drift and KelpDAO, are not here because neither was a Safe multisig with a known threshold.

Method notes: how each chain is read, Zcash, shared control, what this is not

How this differs from the tools you may know. Hypernative and Blockaid monitor threats behind a closed dashboard; Gauntlet, Chaos Labs and LlamaRisk model collateral risk and are paid by the protocols they rate; SolGov, built after the Drift exploit, tracks Solana multisigs on a website; Forta's Risk Graph maps control closure and blast radius on Ethereum mainnet only, behind an OAuth-gated service, with no published score and nothing on-chain; DeFiSafety and DeFiScan publish static reports (DeFiScan stopped in 2026). This page scores one thing only, the authority path (who can change a contract, how many of them, with what delay, who feeds the price), publishes the score on-chain where a contract can read it (getScore, isStale on 8 EVM chains, an account read on Solana, plus a hash commitment on Zcash), re-reads it every 6 hours with a read-only job, and shows the queue of changes before they apply. What those tools do better, and where this one is still thin, is written down in docs/LANDSCAPE.md. Everything here is a file you can download (data / API in the status line), under CC BY 4.0.

Independence. No protocol pays for a score or can buy a change; disputes are public issues with the evidence attached; the data, the rules and the scripts are in the repository.

The oracle on its own scale. The scores are pushed on-chain by one updater key, with no timelock: on this very scale the oracle would score about 4 on the EVM oracles and 2 on Solana. That is why nothing here asks you to trust it: every score can be re-read from the chain in your browser ("verify all live"), the authority chain of every target can be read live ("Read it now from the chain"), and the method hash is on-chain with each score.

What your browser sends. On load, the page fetches the watch files from GitHub (or from the jsDelivr mirror if GitHub does not answer), reads the freshness of the nine oracles on their testnet RPCs, loads protocol and chain logos from the DefiLlama icon CDN, asks the public mainnet RPC of each chain (EVM and Solana) for the name of the few contracts without a written card, and asks openchain.xyz for the names of queued function selectors; about fifty requests in all, none carrying anything about you beyond your IP address (the hosts above see it). The typefaces are embedded in the page: no font host is called. A wallet you paste goes to the public RPC of each chain and, when no tracked token is found on an Ethereum address, to the Blockscout explorer (eth.blockscout.com) to list its other assets; nowhere else. Opening the Zcash tab, and only then, fetches its testnet transactions through the r.jina.ai content proxy, which sees the transaction ids asked and your IP address. Nothing is stored outside this browser (your stars, your rules, your last visit). No analytics, no cookies, no tracking pixel.

This build. Page generated on 2026-10-22 from the dashboard at commit 957621b of the repository; the data it shows is re-read live, the layout is pinned to that commit.

Cite. Authority Risk Oracle, RealSpap, realspap.github.io/oracle, data as of the date shown in the status line; code MIT, data CC BY 4.0.

Every chain tab above reads live, in your browser, straight from getScore(address) on that chain's deployed oracle (selector 0xd47875d0), after enumerating trackedTargets(uint256) (0x9481e5e0) up to trackedTargetsCount() (0x835e2172). Not-applicable sub-scores (e.g. oracleAuthorityScore on a lending vault) read 100 by convention - full marks, not a penalty - rather than being silently omitted. Click a card's Link chip to get a shareable, deep-linkable URL straight to that finding.

The Zcash tab is a genuinely different mechanism, not a smaller version of the EVM one: Zcash has no contract VM, so there's no oracle contract to call. Instead it's a signed, off-chain score attestation with its commitment hash anchored in a real Zcash Testnet OP_RETURN output - this dashboard fetches that transaction, decodes the commitment, and recomputes it from the full attestation live in your browser, rather than trusting either side alone. It verifies three publications: the ARO2 commitment over the six live targets (the Zenrock zenZEC keyring was retired from the live set on 2026-09-20, see its legacy snapshot), the ARO2 whole-set commitment re-anchored from a rotated key, the first ARO2 anchor of the same set (testnet_oracle_batch_2026-09-19.md), and lists the earlier single-score ARO1 proof of concept without re-verifying it, because its attestation file is not part of this public copy. The verified ones prove integrity and timing of the scores, not that the scores are true; the first ARO2 anchor and ARO1 were signed by a publisher key that was later found in the repository's history.

Cross-exposure is a 5th dimension, separate from the composite: it checks whether the same real signer (a bare EOA, or a Gnosis Safe owner) also controls another tracked target, on the same chain or on another ecosystem, reusing this project's multisig-overlap methodology. 100 = no shared signer with any other group; within one ecosystem it drops by 20 per additional group sharing a root signer, and a root committee identical to a tracked target's committee on another ecosystem is capped at a flat 80. The cap is min(within-ecosystem score, 80), so a value already lowered is never raised back, and a scorer compares the owner set it just read against a dated snapshot of the other chain's committee instead of calling a second RPC (the rule is documented once, in METHODOLOGY.md, under "Convention (decided 2026-09-20)"). As of 2026-09-20 the EVM tabs and Tempo fold the committees they hold a dated snapshot of; a target with no snapshot to compare against (for example Arbitrum's GMX and Camelot, or Plasma's validator set and Yuzu) reports 100, which means no overlap was checked for, not that none exists. These values were pushed on-chain on 2026-09-20 to the Ethereum L1, Arbitrum, Plasma, Monad, Tempo and Robinhood Chain oracles (Base had no score change and was not re-pushed), and each oracle now reads back equal to the scorer output; cards whose numbers changed in that push say "pushed on-chain 2026-09-20". On the Arbitrum and Base tabs this caught a real, live finding: Aave's own emergency-guardian Safe is the identical 9-signer committee on both chains, just redeployed at a different address, so one compromised committee reaches both chains' cancel path.

Full methodology, per-target proof files, and the scorer source: the repository. Submitted to Colosseum's Crypto World's Fair on 12 October 2026.
